purpose: Two page-specific appearances of one primary report, prepared as a pilot for the citation-context workflow.

reuseProvenance.note: The existing record supplied the source identity and baseline interpretation. The primary report's relevant sections were accessed again for this pilot; each page's relevance and limitations were written separately. This does not re-review the report's underlying scientific literature.

sectionsRead: Cover and executive summary, printed pages 1–6
Section V.D and V.E, printed pages 53–57
sourceAccess.scopeNote: Targeted passages were read; underlying company exhibits and scientific studies cited by the report were not independently accessed or checked.

records.referenceTitle: Baby Foods Are Tainted with Dangerous Levels of Arsenic, Lead, Cadmium, and Mercury
records.citation: U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Reform, Subcommittee on Economic and Consumer Policy. Staff report, 4 February 2021.
records.summary: Congressional staff examined company testing records for arsenic, lead, cadmium and mercury in baby foods and recommended finished-product testing and public disclosure.
records.establishes: It documents the investigation's four-metal scope. It does not establish a complete testing panel, industry-wide certification practice or subsequent litigation history.
records.relevance: It grounds the briefing's opening discussion of the familiar four metals. The later claim about multidistrict litigation needs a separate court source; the case for testing additional elements rests on the other cited assessments and standards.

sourceLocators: Cover, printed page 1: report title and date
Executive summary, printed pages 2–6: investigation scope and recommendations

pageContexts.claim: The opening identifies the report as a four-metal public-policy reference, then attributes subsequent industry and regulatory anchoring to that frame.
pageContexts.assessment: Supports identifying the four named metals. Industry-wide adoption and causation require additional evidence.

pageContexts.claim: The same reference is attached to a description of those four metals progressing into multidistrict litigation and exhibits.
pageContexts.assessment: The later litigation narrative requires its own court records; the 2021 report cannot establish subsequent proceedings.

evidenceNotes.copyDecision: Reuse the report identity and broad scope; tailor relevance to the briefing's argument about panel breadth. Do not infer that all certification programs test only four metals.
evidenceNotes.publicationStatus: Draft ready for editorial review; page prose remains unchanged.

records.referenceTitle: Baby Foods Are Tainted with Dangerous Levels of Arsenic, Lead, Cadmium, and Mercury
records.citation: U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Reform, Subcommittee on Economic and Consumer Policy. Staff report, 4 February 2021.
records.summary: Congressional staff examined company testing records for arsenic, lead, cadmium and mercury in baby foods and recommended finished-product testing and public disclosure.
records.establishes: The report describes Hain's reliance on ingredient testing and an August 2019 presentation of finished-product results. It does not establish when finished-product testing first began.
records.relevance: It supports the briefing's distinction between brand trust and product verification. Its evidence is narrower than the claim that testing began only in 2019, and does not resolve whether a product caused an individual child's injury.

sourceLocators: Printed page 16: routine ingredient testing versus a small sample of finished products
Printed pages 53–55: August 2019 presentation and ingredient versus finished-product comparison
Printed pages 56–57: testing-policy discussion and supporting footnotes

pageContexts.claim: The page says Earth's Best had not tested its finished products for heavy metals until 2019, as an example of a gap between consumer trust and verification.
pageContexts.assessment: Supports the distinction between routine ingredient testing and finished-product verification. The first-ever testing date is not established by the passages reviewed.

pageContexts.claim: The bibliography repeats the assertion that a major manufacturer had not tested finished products until 2019.
pageContexts.assessment: This repeats the same unsupported chronology; it is not independent corroboration.

evidenceNotes.copyDecision: Use the same source summary, but connect relevance to verification and the specific scope of the testing evidence. Do not introduce numerical contamination results or conclusions about injury causation.
evidenceNotes.publicationStatus: Draft ready for editorial review; page prose remains unchanged.
